title: Michael C. Mozer (@mc_mozer) — thread (4 tweets)
summary:
[1/4] [1/4] As you read words in this text, your brain adjusts fixation durations to facilitate comprehension. Inspired by human reading behavior, we propose a supervised objective that trains an LLM to dynamically determine the number of compute steps for each input token.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G3eNZV_XwAAbDln.jpg
────────
[2/4] [2/4] The model can request additional compute steps for any token by emitting a <don't know> output. If the model is granted a delay, a <pause> token is inserted at the next input step, providing the model with additional compute resources to generate an output.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G3eNyoeXsAAthfH.jpg
────────
[3/4] [3/4] To train the model to calibrate its uncertainty and use <don't know> outputs judiciously, we frame the selection of each output token as a sequential-decision problem with a time penalty. We refer to the class of methods as “Catch Your Breath” losses.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G3eOAvAWYAAjkMJ.jpg
────────
[4/4] [4/4] Details and results found at (Catch Your Breath: Adaptive Computation for Self-Paced Sequence Production). Joint work with @agalashov , @rosemary_ke, @caoyuan33, @_vaishnavh, and Matt Jones.

title: Michael C. Mozer (@mc_mozer) — thread (5 tweets)
summary:
[1/5] [1/5] Intelligent behavior relies on maintaining an evolving, dynamic model of the environment. But even frontier models sometimes fail at tracking state in dialogs, e.g., actual transcript from 4/20/2026:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGdcDICa8AA7VBK.jpg
────────
[2/5] [3/5] Because activations in the transformer flow in one direction, evolving state representations are pushed deeper into their layer stack. As a result, vital information is inaccessible to shallower layers, and ultimately the model’s depthis exhausted.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGdcdWTbsAAdMVx.png
────────
[3/5] [2/5] In @ShoaibASiddiqui, @savvyRL, and I explain why feedforward transformer architectures are fundamentally ill suited to complex state-tracking tasks.
────────
[4/5] [4/5] Recurrence is an obvious solution, but the literature often conflates qualitatively different varieties of recurrence in transformers, some of which enable indefinite state tracking and others (particularly, variants of looped transformers) do not.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGdcthoa0AAC7Wz.jpg
────────
[5/5] [5/5] We introduce a taxonomy of recurrent models defined by their recurrence axis and their ratio of input tokens to recurrence steps. The next generation of efficient foundation models need to bridge the gap between a transformer's parallelism and the brain's dynamical nature.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGddjyqbEAATu-L.jpg

title: Michael C. Mozer (@mc_mozer) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] What if a foundation model could tell us how to modify its architecture to boost inference and reasoning instantaneously—without retraining? What if that tweak incurred near zero latency cost during generation and supported indefinite state tracking?
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/HQHsA2ebcAAqafE.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/tweet_video/HQHsA2ebcAAqafE.mp4
────────
[2/2] We introduce an inference-time recurrence mechanism that allows off-the-shelf, frozen LLMs to act as dynamical systems. By leaking deep representations back to shallow layers, we see bonkers gains—23% ⬇️ in perplexity, 21% ⬆️ rel. accuracy in GSM8k— w/o touching model weights.

title: Michael C. Mozer (@mc_mozer)
clean_title: Agentic meta-reasoning lets models structure their own computation
summary:
What if an agent could decide how to structure its own computation?
Agentic Meta-Reasoning: Let the model decide what to explore, what to build on, what to verify, and where to spend its next unit of compute: effectively constructing its own computational graph as it reasons. 🧵
Paras Dahal, @anton_bakhtin , @TacoCohen , Zhengxing Chen, Carole-Jean Wu, Rob Fergus, Scott Yih, @syhw , @rsalakhu , @prfsanjeevarora , @jaseweston
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTfBnkTbQAAtBPp.jpg
clean_summary:
Usually, models follow a fixed process when they compute answers, spending their resources in a preset way. But what if a model could decide for itself what to explore, what to build on, and where to spend its next unit of compute?

Michael C. Mozer shares work on agentic meta-reasoning, where the model effectively constructs its own computational graph as it reasons. This means the model dynamically chooses its next steps, potentially making its reasoning more efficient and focused.
